tip: 'Belum' means 'not yet' and implies it will still happen: 'Saya belum sarapan' = I haven't had breakfast yet. Even 'are you married?' is normally answered with 'belum', not 'tidak'.
'Belum', not 'tidak': 'belum pulang' = not home yet, still expected. 'Tidak pulang' would mean he isn't coming home at all.
'Sedang' marks action in progress: 'Ibu sedang memasak' (Mom is cooking right now).
'Akan' puts a sentence in the future without touching the verb: 'Saya akan pergi' = I will go. 'Pergi' keeps the same form in past, present, and future.
'Akan' is optional once a time word sets the future – with 'bulan depan' in the sentence, 'Dia mulai pekerjaan baru bulan depan' works fine too.
'Sebentar lagi' is literally 'a moment more' – 'lagi' after a time span means that far from now: 'seminggu lagi' = in a week.
'Baru' literally means new – 'baru saja bangun' is 'newly woke up', so 'baru saja' before a verb = just did it.
'Masih' = still, the action continues: 'Dia masih bekerja' (He is still working).
'Pernah' = have ever done at least once: 'Saya pernah ke Bali' (I have been to Bali).
'Belum pernah' = never so far: 'Dia belum pernah naik pesawat' (He has never flown).
Question words can stay in place: 'Kamu tinggal di mana?' is literally 'You live where?' – unlike English, 'di mana' doesn't have to move to the front.
'Ke mana' asks where to (motion): 'Ke mana kamu pergi?' (Where are you going?)
Destination questions can drop the verb: 'Bus ini ke mana?' (Where does this bus go?)
Tens stack simply: 'lima puluh' = five tens = 50, 'dua puluh' = 20.
'Harganya' = 'harga' + '-nya' ('its price'): 'Kopi ini harganya...' is literally 'This coffee, its price 25 thousand' – no verb needed.
'Ada' = there is/are: 'Ada empat orang' (There are four people).
After 'mau', the bare root is natural in speech: 'mau beli' = want to buy.
'Se-' often means one: 'seratus' = one hundred, 'semalam' = one night.
Order matters: 'jam berapa' = what time, 'berapa jam' = how many hours. 'Jam berapa sekarang?' asks for the clock time, not a duration.
Time of day follows the hour: 'jam sembilan pagi' = 9 a.m., 'jam sembilan malam' = 9 p.m.
'Sore' = late afternoon, about 3-6 p.m.: 'jam tiga sore' = 3 p.m.
Days usually take 'hari' first: 'hari Senin' = Monday, 'hari Sabtu' = Saturday.
Before 'c', 'meN-' becomes 'men-': 'cuci' → 'mencuci' (wash).
Roots starting with 'm' keep a simple 'me-': 'masak' → 'memasak' (cook).
Before 't', 'meN-' becomes 'men-' and the 't' drops: 'tulis' → 'menulis' (write).
Before 'b', 'meN-' becomes 'mem-' and the 'b' stays: 'baca' → 'membaca' (read).
Before 's', 'meN-' becomes 'meny-' and the 's' drops: 'sapu' → 'menyapu' (sweep).
Vowel-first roots take 'meng-': 'ambil' → 'mengambil' (take).
Indonesian verbs never change for -ing – 'sedang' does the job: 'sedang membaca' = in the middle of reading. Drop 'sedang' and it just means 'read'.
No past tense here – 'sudah bangun' is literally 'already wake'. 'Sudah' marks the action as finished; the verb 'bangun' itself never changes for tense.
